database.title: Matrix Synapse
database.blurb: The reference Matrix homeserver. This is the full schema at schema version 72 (the main and state stores together), which is the only complete schema the project publishes; every change after it ships as a delta, so this is the version-72 picture rather than the current one. Synapse declares almost no primary keys and almost no foreign keys: rows are identified by unique indexes and the server keeps them consistent itself.

conventions: Row identity comes from unique indexes, not declared primary keys. 88 of the 109 tables the reviewer flags carry one; the remaining 21 are append-only streams, edge tables and queues with no uniqueness enforced at all.
Relationships are not declared as foreign keys. Only 14 exist across 137 tables; the rest are joins by convention on user_id, room_id, event_id and stream_ordering.
Ordering is by monotonic stream_ordering / stream_id columns rather than timestamps, so workers can resume from a position.
Timestamps are bigint milliseconds since the epoch (ts, created_ts, expiry_time_ms), not timestamptz.
Text columns holding a Matrix type (events.type, event_relations.relation_type) are open namespaces defined by the Matrix specification, not closed enumerations.

domains.title: Accounts and identity
domains.blurb: Local accounts, profiles, third-party identifiers (email and phone), registration tokens, and the flags for deactivated or erased users.

domains.title: Sessions and tokens
domains.blurb: How a client proves who it is: access and refresh tokens, OpenID tokens, and the multi-stage interactive auth sessions used for login and account changes.

domains.title: Devices and device lists
domains.blurb: One row per logged-in device, the to-device message inbox, and the machinery that tells other servers when a user's device list changes.

domains.title: End-to-end encryption
domains.blurb: Device keys, one-time and fallback keys, cross-signing keys and signatures, and server-side room key backups.

domains.title: Rooms and membership
domains.blurb: Rooms, their aliases, who is in them, per-room tags and account data, retention policy and the server-level block list.

domains.title: The event graph
domains.blurb: The heart of a homeserver: every event, its JSON, the directed acyclic graph edges that order it, the authorisation chains, and the extremities that mark the current frontier.

domains.title: Room state
domains.blurb: Resolved room state: state groups and the edges between them, the state each group holds, and the current state of every room.

domains.title: Federation
domains.blurb: Talking to other homeservers: destinations and their retry state, received transactions, staged inbound events, remote server signing keys, and partial-state rooms during a fast join.

domains.title: Application services
domains.blurb: Bridges and bots: per-service transaction state and the rooms each service has claimed.

domains.title: Push notifications
domains.blurb: Registered pushers, the rules deciding what is worth notifying about, and the per-user unread and highlight counts kept alongside them.

domains.title: Receipts and presence
domains.blurb: Read receipts in both graph and linearised form, and who is online.

domains.title: Media repository
domains.blurb: Locally uploaded files and cached remote ones, their generated thumbnails, and the URL preview cache.

domains.title: User directory and statistics
domains.blurb: The searchable user directory, which users share rooms, and the rolled-up room and user statistics behind the admin views.

domains.title: Worker coordination
domains.blurb: How the processes that make up one homeserver stay in step: worker locks, the instance map, stream positions and cache invalidation, plus per-user rate-limit overrides.

Not a polymorphic pair. `room_id` is this table's own key (unique index on room_id) and `room_type` is the Matrix room type, such as m.space, not a discriminator naming another table.

Not a polymorphic pair. (session_type, session_id) is the composite key of a generic key-value session store whose payload is an opaque `value` column; session_type namespaces the id rather than naming a parent table.

The pair cannot be duplicated: there is a unique index on `event_id` alone, which is stricter than uniqueness across (event_id, room_id). The finding's claim that the same pair can be inserted twice does not hold for this table.
